k001: DumbMonit: dumb-simple monitoring from the homelab to the small business
k013: Is everything fine? Know in one second.
k014: Dumb-simple, self-hosted monitoring from the homelab to the small business. One container, one IP address to type in, useful graphs and alerts in under a minute.
k016: Then open http://localhost:8080 and create the first account. Image for amd64 (arm64 later): ghcr.io/laupernoe/dumbmonit.
k020: The bulletin, on the wall screen of a test instance with failures switched on — the weather window is a living Paris rooftop with the pigeons. On a quiet day it reads “Clear skies.”
k021: This is an alpha (0.1.0-alpha.7 is the current release). DumbMonit runs every day on its author's own network, but the HTTP API is not frozen, the database schema still moves and there is no upgrade guarantee across schema changes yet. Several integrations have only met test instances, not years-old production hardware; they are marked below. Try it, and tell us what breaks.
k023: The device list (Monitors) shows rows or tiles with product icons. Pick a monitor type among more than fifty, read the notice that says what to prepare on the device, fill in only the fields that type needs. SNMP profiles are picked from the device's sysObjectID; defaults do the rest.
k025: SNMP v1, v2c and v3Switches, routers, NAS, UPS, printers. Interfaces and errors, host resources, UPS battery, printer supplies; seven profiles ship and apply themselves.
k026: OPNsense Test instance onlyGateways with round-trip time and loss, the pf state table, VPN tunnels, DHCP leases, CARP, pending updates. Read-only API key.
k027: Network discoverySweep a CIDR range and add everything that answers in one go.
k029: Proxmox VENodes, VMs and containers, storage, HA, Ceph, ZFS, cluster quorum, and the age of the last backup of every guest.
k030: Proxmox Datacenter Manager Test instance onlyWhich clusters and backup servers the console still reaches, the whole estate on one page, failed tasks on every site.
k031: Server hardware (Redfish) Reference mockups onlyFans, temperatures against the hardware's own thresholds, power supplies and redundancy, drives, memory, the event log. Checked against the DMTF mockups, not yet a real iDRAC, iLO or Supermicro board.
k032: Machines with the agentLinux and Windows, with macOS and FreeBSD in preview. More below.
k033: Active DirectoryA Windows domain over LDAP with a plain, unprivileged account: FSMO roles, privileged groups, and the facts a domain audit looks for first — Kerberoastable accounts, old krbtgt password, computers without LAPS.
k035: Proxmox Backup ServerA 30-day backup calendar per machine, failed tasks with their logs, verify and GC jobs, datastore fill-up forecast.
k036: Synology DSMVolumes, pools, disks and SMART, temperature, Hyper Backup and Active Backup for Business with the age of the last success, plus Drive and Photos package status.
k037: TrueNAS Test instance onlyThe pool that lost a disk and still serves data, with the disk named; scrubs, quotas, snapshots, replication, SMART.
k038: Plakar backupsAge and result of the last snapshot per repository, through the agent.
k040: Uptime checksHTTP(S) with status, keyword, JSON path and certificate; TCP port; DNS records; ping; TLS certificate expiry; NTP offset and stratum. History bar, response time, availability.
k041: Application sessionsSMTP, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, MQTT and WebSocket: a real login or handshake, so “up but refusing you” is not reported as “up”.
k042: HeartbeatsA cron job or backup script calls a secret URL; when it stops calling, you hear about it. Uptime Kuma push-compatible.
k043: Docker containersState, health, restarts, image age and available updates, through the agent. Opt-in restart and update inside a maintenance window.
k044: Website health & SEODown, error, blank page, missing expected text, noindex, a robots.txt blocking everything, slow answers, and changes of title, description or canonical URL (confirmed by two checks in a row). Redirects are followed, so http to https is not a false alarm. Also catches a page that turns nearly empty, changes of language tags and redirects, with each check switchable and the confirmation count adjustable. Sites get a category (e-commerce, blog, web app, showcase) and a platform (WordPress, Shopify, Wix…). Built for hundreds of sites: probes are spread over the interval and polite to each domain, and a CSV import files them in folders.
k045: Website change detectionWatch a page, or a whole site crawled from its sitemap, for changes in its visible text: before/after text, a line diff and, when available, screenshots.
k046: GitLab and Forgejo/GiteaSidekiq queues, CI/CD runners, scheduled tasks and database migrations on a self-managed Git forge. An ordinary access token proves the instance is up.
k047: Nginx and ApacheActive/idle workers or connections, request and byte rates, through stub_status or mod_status. No account needed.
k048: Proxmox Mail Gateway Test instance onlyPostfix queues and the oldest stuck message, mail filtered today, quarantine sizes, the age of antivirus and antispam signatures.
k050: Test instance onlyBuilt and checked against a real copy of the software installed for the purpose, not yet run for weeks in production
k051: Every kind has its own page in the monitor documentation, with exactly what it reads and what to prepare. A demo monitor kind produces data without any hardware.
k052: Adding a monitor: pick a type, and the notice on the right says what to prepare.
k053: Proxmox VE: every guest, its disk and its last backup.
k054: Proxmox Backup Server: the backup that stopped running, found before restore day.
k056: Useful rules are on right after install. The work goes into sending fewer, better messages.
k058: Declare a switch as the parent of what sits behind it. When it goes down you get one notification, not thirty; the others read “Suppressed by parent”.
k060: A NAS whose array degrades sends one message per cycle, not one per disk. Reminders, escalation, acknowledgement, snooze, per-device ignore and clearing resolved history are all built in.
k062: Anomaly detection with no threshold to tune: 168 buckets, one per hour of the week. It stays silent for its first 14 days and only shows what it would have fired.
k064: “This filesystem will be full within four days” is listed as a forecast, apart from what is broken right now.
k066: One-off or weekly windows, hysteresis, flap hold, quiet hours, batching and an hourly cap, so a bad night does not become two hundred pushes.
k068: Alerts, grouped by host. Severities read like a weather service: info, advisory, warning.
k070: Each one has a Test button and a setup page in the documentation.
k093: An agent for what does not speak SNMP
k094: A small binary that pushes CPU, memory, disks, network, services and uptime to the server, plus temperatures, fans, SMART and ZFS pools where the machine exposes them. It calls the server, never the other way round: no port to open on the machine.
k095: A PowerShell script is served at /install.ps1 for Windows. The agent is also an image, ghcr.io/laupernoe/dumbmonit-agent.
k098: x86_64 and aarch64, systemd or OpenRC. Docker containers and OS health (updates, pending reboot, failed units).
k100: x86_64, installed as a Windows service. SMART through smartctl.
k103: launchd, Apple silicon and Intel; binaries attached to each release. Not yet run on real hardware.
k105: rc.d, x86_64, ZFS pools. Not yet run on real hardware.
k107: In relay mode an agent runs the server's probes (SNMP, Proxmox, HTTP…) from its own network — a second site, a client's network or a VPS behind NAT — with nothing inbound: no VPN, no port to open. Monitor a remote site
k108: Status pages for the people you serve
k109: Public pages at /s/<name>: groups of services with 90 days of daily history, 30- and 90-day uptime, incident and maintenance announcements, email subscribers with double opt-in, RSS, badges for a README, a compact embed for an intranet, an optional 90-day calendar and response-time graphs, and an optional scene behind the banner: about fifty to pick from, from city skylines (Venice, Paris, Tokyo, New York…) and wonders of the world to Swiss landmarks (the Matterhorn, the Jet d’Eau, Lucerne, Bern, Chillon). The sky follows the state of your services, and each scene reacts in its own way when something goes down or comes back. The Swiss ones carry an SBB-style station clock, a split-flap alert board, fireworks on 1 August, the Escalade cauldron and winter snow.
k110: Only the labels you choose leave the server. Device names, addresses and types never appear on the page, in a badge or in an email.
k113: The bulletin alone, full screen, for a room monitor: a living scene (Paris rooftop with the Eiffel Tower and the DumbMonit pigeons by default, or one of many others) whose weather follows your alerts, an OLED theme for a screen left on for days, and wall music — Spotify Connect turns the screen into a speaker.
k115: Every supported device gets a 0–100 score and an A–F grade from the vendor’s own best-practice checks, PingCastle-style: category, severity, evidence, remediation, and a worst-first Security page.
k117: Admin, operator (handles alerts, changes no configuration) and viewer roles, optional TOTP second factor, an audit log, and single sign-on over OpenID Connect (Authentik, Authelia, Keycloak, Pocket ID…), account creation off by default.
k118: Plays well with what you run
k119: /metrics, /federate and a Prometheus-compatible endpoint let an existing Grafana read DumbMonit's data.
k121: Every route behind /api/openapi.json (OpenAPI 3.1): scoped tokens (dmt_…, read or write) that can expire, be restricted to a network, and are rate-limited. API reference
k123: 27 tools for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, VS Code or Cursor: read status, devices, alerts, metrics and agents; a write token can also silence, acknowledge, add a device or restart a container. Secrets never come back. Connect an assistant
k125: Read the state, acknowledge an alert, start a maintenance window. Installable on the home screen, deliberately without an offline mode: it never shows yesterday's state.
k126: The same bulletin at phone width.
k127: Small enough to forget it is there
k128: One Rust binary with the web interface built in, the VictoriaMetrics time-series database started by that binary inside the same image, and SQLite for configuration. No database container, no message queue.
k136: The memory figure is the whole container, time-series database included, on a small instance. The database's cache budget is 256 MB by default and can be raised for hundreds of hosts.
k137: Runs as a non-root user on a read-only file system, with every capability dropped. Ping monitors work through a sysctl, not NET_RAW.
k138: Redirects followed by probes and notification channels never leave the configured host, a channel cannot be pointed at DumbMonit itself, and webhook headers are stored as encrypted secrets.
k139: Credentials are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM). Backups are one file, encrypted with a passphrase you choose, restorable onto a fresh instance with a dry run first.
k140: Already running VictoriaMetrics? Point DUMBMONIT_VM_URL at it and the embedded one is not started.
k142: DumbMonit is for people who watch ten machines and three switches. The established tools are excellent at what they do; here is where each one fits better.
k144: Mature, proven on thousands of hosts, with a template for nearly everything, distributed proxies and long-term support releases. It also asks for a database server, a web front end and time to learn items, triggers and templates.
k145: Choose Zabbix for large fleets or when you need that depth today. Choose DumbMonit when you want the one-second answer and can live with fewer integrations and a young project.
k147: The standard for metrics: a huge exporter ecosystem, PromQL and dashboards for anything, including your own applications. You assemble and maintain the stack yourself: Prometheus, Alertmanager, exporters, dashboards and rules.
k148: DumbMonit ships that assembly already done, and exposes /metrics, /federate and a Prometheus-compatible endpoint, so the two can live side by side.
k150: A polished, very popular uptime monitor with more monitor types, more notification services and a larger community. It checks services from the outside; it does not read a switch's ports, a hypervisor's guests or a NAS's disks.
k151: DumbMonit includes Kuma-style checks and push-compatible heartbeats, next to device metrics. If uptime checks are all you need, Uptime Kuma is the more mature choice.
k153: Apache 2.0, dependencies included: CI fails on any dependency that is not under an OSI-approved licence. No feature is held back for a paid edition, because there is none.
k154: This site has no analytics, no cookies and no third-party requests.
k156: The HTTP API is not frozen and the database schema still changes between alphas.
k157: OPNsense, TrueNAS, Proxmox Datacenter Manager and Mail Gateway need reports from real, long-running installs. Redfish needs a real management controller.
k158: The macOS and FreeBSD agents need someone to run them on real hardware.
k159: The interface is in English; the language picker already offers 8 more (German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese in two variants, Russian, Simplified Chinese), partly translated (the documentation is available in the same languages), and translations are open on Weblate.
k160: What gets built next is decided in the GitHub issues, and the changelog says what changed.
k162: A device that reads wrong, an alert that woke you for nothing, a page that confused you: each report makes the next alpha better. Device support requests are welcome too.
k165: DumbMonit, Apache 2.0. The mascot is a pigeon.
